references.text: In [ref:2 Krøn 36:15-16|2 Chronicles 36:15-16], it is described how God repeatedly sent His messengers to the people, but they were mocked, despised, and mistreated—the same pattern of repeated sending and rejection as in Jesus' parable.
[ref:Neh 9:26|Nehemiah 9:26] tells how the people of Israel killed the prophets who testified against them, reflecting the vineyard workers' treatment of the third servant.

In [ref:Jer 20:2|Jeremiah 20:2], the prophet Jeremiah was beaten and put in stocks—an example of God's messengers being mistreated (τραυματίσαντες), just as the third servant in the parable was wounded and cast out.
[ref:Jes 5:1-5|Isaiah 5:1-5] is the original vineyard parable that forms the background for Jesus' parable, where God repeatedly tries to get fruit from His people without result.

[ref:Luk 20:10-11|Luke 20:10-11] describes the two preceding servants who were also mistreated and sent away empty-handed, showing the escalating pattern that culminates with the third servant in verse 12.

In [ref:Mark 12:4-5|Mark 12:4-5], Mark's parallel account tells of several servants who were beaten, wounded, and killed—an expanded version of the same motif of repeated rejection of God's messengers.
[ref:Matt 21:35-36|Matthew 21:35-36] is Matthew's parallel where the vineyard workers beat, killed, and stoned the servants, and then treated a new group in the same way.

In [ref:Matt 23:37|Matthew 23:37], Jesus laments over Jerusalem for killing the prophets and stoning those sent to the city—a clear expression of God's repeated attempts to reach His people, just as the owner of the vineyard sent the third servant.

[ref:Apg 7:52|Acts 7:52] summarizes Stephen's speech in which he accuses the people of having persecuted and killed the prophets—the historical reality behind the parable's image of the mistreated servants.

[ref:1 Tess 2:15|1 Thessalonians 2:15] refers to those who killed the Lord Jesus and the prophets and persecuted the apostles, confirming the pattern of rejection of God's messengers that the parable illustrates.
